::: {#first-column width="35%"}

One funny thing about me is that I actually can’t pinpoint the moment or series of moments that drove me to care for the health of the environment and communities. Often environmental scientists have tales of childhoods spent outside — and although I did spend a lot of time outside — my desire to study and work in the environmental field didn’t come around until college. 

I started at Wesleyan University with a dream to be a journalist (after a childhood of English being my best subject), but that idea was squashed when I realized that I did not care for my introductory government class. In my attempt to explore all potential paths (bless Wesleyan’s open curriculum), I took a class on renewable energy, and that’s what ended up sticking. In undergrad I took courses in soils, geobiology, sedimentology, planetary evolution, studied abroad on the Galápagos Islands and in New Zealand, and did a capstone project on ant species in Puerto Rico. Truly the most enriching parts of my education were all of the afternoons I spent in the field, learning how the world works. 

At the same time, I was also completing an economics major — learning about statistical methods and the science of choice. Though it did not make me light up like digging for fossils at an abandoned quarry, I still liked it. It felt pragmatic, another way of making sense of the world. The major was also my first introduction to coding, as I got to learn Stata, a statistical software which, in the economics field, is used as often as R. 

After finishing my Bachelor’s degree, I — perhaps in an attempt to delay the job search — shipped out to California to pursue a Master of Environmental Data Science at UCSB. I hoped this intersection of environment and economics is where I could belong. Turns out, I love it! Though I still cherish getting my hands dirty and my feet wet, the satisfaction of your code finally running properly after hours of tinkering is hard to beat.

So, my love for walkable cities could come from my first few years of life (and many summers after that) living in Riga, Latvia’s capital city. My excitement for plants and animals and clean air and oceans could come from always living near a coast, or being surrounded by the green of the American, northeastern suburbs. I don’t know. But I do know that I love it all, and I want to use both my passion and skills to help make this world run cleaner for the communities — human or not — that inhabit it.

<h2>Research and Professional Experience</h2>

<h3>About Me</h3>

I grew up in southern Connecticut, and ended up at Wesleyan University for my undergraduate education. I double-majored in Earth & Environmnetal Sciences and Economics, and am continuously surprised at how interconnected the two fields are. 

Some of my past projects include exploring evolutionary divergence of fish species, trophic levels of ants in Puerto Rico, and testing for bacteria concentrations at a water quality monitoring organization.

In my free time, I enjoy hiking, swimming, reading, and doing little crafts like crocheting and sewing. I'm also a big fan of the Great British Baking Show and Bad Bunny. Current personal projects include practicing my Spanish (I traveled to Argentina this winter and was able to get around!) and potentially running another half marathon soon.
